content.title: Northern Lights Alert: 20 States May See Aurora On Saturday
content.text: NOAA is forecasting a G1 or G2-class geomagnetic storm on Saturday, April 4, through Sunday, April 5, with aurora possible from northern U.S. states and Canada. . (Photo by Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)Anadolu via Getty ImagesThe northern lights may be seen in up to 20 U.S. states Saturday, April 4, through Sunday, April 5, after the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) issued a geomagnetic storm watch, warning that minor G1 or moderate G2-class geomagnetic storms are possible. That may mean auroras being seen in the northern sky from northern U.S. states. According to NOAA, the geomagnetic field is expected to reach G1 storm levels on April 4, with periods of G2 storming likely, “due to waning CME effects and negative polarity CH HSS influences.” That refers to a coronal mass ejection — a cloud of charged particles — which struck Earth’s magnetic field on April 3 and caused a strong geomagnetic storm, as well as a high-speed stream of solar wind from a hole in the sun’s corona, which continues to interact with Earth’s magnetic field. Periods of active conditions are also expected on April 5, according to NOAA. A bright 90%-lit waning gibbous moon will rise after midnight, making conditions less than ideal for seeing faint aurora in the middle of the night. ForbesNorthern Lights Alert: 10 States Could See Easter Aurora This WeekendNorthern Lights Alert: Where And When To LookThe northern lights will potentially be visible — most likely low on the northern horizon — in up to 10 U.S. states near the Canada border. States in pole position include Alaska and (northerly parts of) Washington, Idaho, Montana, North Dakota, South Dakota, Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan and Maine.If a G2-class geomagnetic storm erupts — which is possible — it could potentially make aurora viewable from states much farther south. That could mean faint auroras visible low on the northern horizon in northern regions of Oregon, Wyoming, Nebraska, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, New York, Vermont and New Hampshire. However, states farther north will always have the best odds.Until moonrise, the best views will be from regions with low levels of light pollution, which can be identified using a light pollution map and a Dark Sky Place Finder (though finding a clear sky will also be essential). The clearer and darker the northern sky, the more vibrant the display — even during moderate geomagnetic storms. ForbesAstronauts Share Spectacular Earth Images From Halfway To The MoonBy Jamie Carter Northern Lights Alert: Latest UpdatesThe exact timing of space weather is difficult to predict because it depends on the speed of the solar wind. Continually monitor NOAA’s 30-minute aurora forecast and SpaceWeatherLive.com, as well as apps such as Aurora Now, My Aurora Forecast, SpaceWeatherLive or Glendale Aurora, which provide live solar wind data.Look for data on the interplanetary magnetic field’s Bz component, which determines how easily solar energy enters Earth’s magnetosphere. When Bz points north, Earth’s field resists it; when Bz swings south, the two fields connect, allowing plasma to stream in. A sustained southward Bz of -5 nT or stronger usually signals an imminent display of aurora.How To Photograph The Northern LightsIf your smartphone has a Night Mode or Pro Mode, you can capture a beautiful aurora photo with these steps:Use your main lens, not the ultra-wide, for sharper results.Stabilize the camera using a tripod or rest it on a firm surface such as a car roof, wall, or post.Shoot in RAW format if available, as it makes post-editing easier.Expect long exposures between five and ten seconds. Even faint glows that look grayish to the eye often appear vividly green, purple or red in photos.Forbes11,000 Asteroids Have Just Been Found — 33 Are Near-Earth ObjectsBy Jamie CarterThe Sun’s 27-Day RotationAurora forecasters often look to the sun’s 27-day rotation as a powerful predictive tool. The sun spins once on its axis roughly every 27 Earth days, carrying sunspots and active regions from right to left as seen from the Northern Hemisphere. If there’s a vast region of active sunspots that cause solar flares and CMEs, predicting when they will return to face Earth again helps space weather forecasters predict renewed geomagnetic disturbances. What Causes The Northern LightsThe solar wind — streams of charged particles flowing from the sun and interacting with Earth’s magnetic field — causes the Northern Lights. While most are deflected, some particles spiral along magnetic field lines toward the poles, colliding with oxygen and nitrogen atoms high in the atmosphere. These collisions excite the gases, causing them to release energy as shimmering light.Wishing you clear skies and wide eyes.
